source_text: Hanc ergo subtilitatem divisionum non introspiciens Manichaeus, Traducianorum nobis produxit examina. Argumentatur enim hoc modo: Unde malum? Nimirum de voluntate. Unde voluntas mala? Respondet: De homine. Unde homo? Per Deum. Concluditque: Si malum ex homine, homo per Deum, malum igitur per Deum. Et post hoc, quasi religiosus, ne criminosum faciat Deum, dat tenebrarum naturam, cui malum debeamus adscribere. Hinc et Augustinus: Unde malum? De voluntate. Unde, inquit, ipsa voluntas? De homine, qui est opus Dei. Et colligit: Si malum ex voluntate, voluntas ex homine, homo opus Dei; malum igitur per Deum. Quod quasi conatus absolvere, ne Deum criminosum dicere videretur (quod tradux eius affirmat), violentum aeque pro Deo nobis nihil obtulit, id est, tenebras quibus malum hoc adscribere deberemus. Non enim, inquit, ideo in homine malum natum est, quia opus Dei erat, sed ideo quia de nihilo erat [n94] . Quasi veritas respondere non possit: Et qua impudentia primo mentitur Deus tuus esse in homine voluntatem; deinde condemnat, cum malum istud, videlicet peccatum, de necessitate noverit tenebrarum, id est, antiqui nihili contigisse? Infleximus per casus nihil, ut appareret Traduciani virtus in nihilo collocantis spem suam. Vide tamen imbecillitatem Dei, quem Traducianus inducit. Ipsum nihilum superare non valuit; cumque hominem fecisset ex nihilo, non eum potuit a conditione mali, quae de nihilo veniebat, exuere; sed rerum difficultate factus amarior, pro suis culpis hominem criminatur, et imaginis suae exitio nihili delicta condemnat. Benignius cum eo agit senex Manes, ut dicat illum non usquequaque tenebrarum gente vastatum; cuius debilitatem tantam inducit Traducianus, ut commentetur eum a nihilo fuisse superatum.
pass_a_gloss: Manichaeus therefore, not looking into this subtlety of divisions, produced for us swarms of Traducians. For he argues in this manner: From where evil? Namely from will. From where an evil will? He replies: From the human. From where the human? Through God. And he concludes: If evil from the human, the human through God, evil therefore through God. And after this, as if religious, lest he make God criminal, he gives a nature of darkness, to which we ought to ascribe evil. From here also Augustine: From where evil? From will. From where, he says, the will itself? From the human, who is a work of God. And he gathers: If evil from will, will from the human, the human a work of God; evil therefore through God. Which as if having tried to finish, lest he seem to say God criminal (which his tradux affirms), he equally offered us a violent nothing in God's place, that is darknesses to which we ought to ascribe this evil. For not, he says, therefore was evil born in the human, because he was a work of God, but therefore because he was from nothing. As if truth could not reply: And by what shamelessness first does your God lie that there is will in the human; then he condemns, when he knows that this evil, namely sin, happened from a necessity of darkness, that is of the ancient nothing? We inflected nothing through cases, that the Traducian's virtue of placing his hope in nothing might appear. See nevertheless the weakness of the God whom the Traducian introduces. He was not able to overcome nothing itself; and when he had made the human from nothing, he could not strip him from the condition of evil which was coming from nothing; but made more bitter by the difficulty of things, he accuses the human for his own faults, and by the destruction of his image condemns the offenses of nothing. The old man Manes acts more kindly with him, that he may say he was not through and through wasted by the nation of darkness; whose so great weakness the Traducian introduces, that he invents him to have been overcome by nothing.

pass_b_english: Failing to perceive this subtle distinction, Mani produced swarms of advocates of inherited sin for us. He argues as follows: ‘Where does evil come from? From will, of course. Where does evil will come from?’ He answers, ‘From a human being. Where does the human being come from? Through God.’ He concludes: ‘If evil comes from a human being, and the human being through God, evil therefore comes through God.’ Then, as though religiously avoiding making God criminal, he supplies a nature of darkness to which we should attribute evil. Augustine follows: ‘Where does evil come from? From will. Where,’ he asks, ‘does that will itself come from? From a human being, who is God’s work.’ He concludes: ‘If evil comes from will, will from a human being, and the human being is God’s work, evil therefore comes through God.’ As though trying to solve this without appearing to call God criminal—which his doctrine of transmission affirms—he offers us, in God’s place, an equally violent nothing: that is, darkness, to which we should attribute this evil. ‘For evil arose in a human being,’ he says, ‘not because he was God’s work, but because he was from nothing’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.28.48).

As though truth could not answer: with what shamelessness does your God first lie that a human being has a will, and then condemn him, when God knows this evil, sin, arose from the necessity of darkness—that is, ancient nothing? I have declined ‘nothing’ through its grammatical cases to display the prowess of the advocate of inherited sin, who places his hope in nothing. But see the weakness of the God he introduces. He could not overcome even nothing. Having made a human being from nothing, he could not free him from the condition of evil that came from nothing. Instead, embittered by the difficulty of affairs, he accuses the human being for his own faults and condemns nothing’s offenses by destroying his own image. Old Mani treats him more kindly, saying that the race of darkness did not ravage him completely. The advocate of inherited sin introduces so great a weakness in God that he invents the claim that God was defeated by nothing.

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
